observations:
All conceptual domains in Torah #2 are well-represented by the seven proposed packages and can be accommodated within them. No independent bechina domain of 3+ concepts was found that is structurally separate from the existing packages.

The four gap concepts identified (יִרְאַת ה', קַשְׁתִּי, בְּתוּלוֹת, עִבּוּר) each attach naturally to existing packages: יִרְאַת ה' and קַשְׁתִּי extend Package 1 (Prayer/Mashiach); בְּתוּלוֹת and עִבּוּר extend Package 2 (Torah/Souls). They do not form an independent thematic family.

The concept of הַסְתָּרַת פָּנִים (divine concealment) is already thematically contained within Package 7 (Chesed and Din in Exile) — it is the overarching state of which פָּנֶיךָ/רַחֲמִים and פָּנָה עֹרֶף/דִּין are the two aspects.

The Torah's argument follows a clear four-stage structure, each stage corresponding to a thematic domain that became a package:
  Stage 1 — Prayer as weapon of Mashiach [Package 1: good]
  Stage 2 — Torah/souls as fuel for prayer [Package 2: good]
  Stage 3 — Mishpat/Jacob as the calibration mechanism [Package 3: good]
  Stage 4 — Shmirat habrit/Yosef as the prerequisite vessel [Package 4: good]
  Stage 5 — Zivug of Shechina as the eschatological goal [Package 5: good]
  Stage 6 — Corruption of mishpat as the evil that blocks prayer [Package 6: evil — mirror of Package 3]
  Stage 7 — Divine chesed/din/rachamin in exile as the structural frame [Package 7: neutral]

The good/evil mirror structure is present: Package 6 (Corruption of Mishpat + Foreign Thoughts) is the exact evil counterpart of Package 3 (Mishpat + Jacob). Where Package 3 describes the clear eyes of Jacob seeing straight through the middle column, Package 6 describes bribery blinding those eyes and clouds covering them, producing foreign thoughts in prayer. This is the primary evil package in Torah #2.

No secondary evil mirror was found for Packages 1, 2, 4, or 5 — Torah #2 does not explicitly develop evil counterparts for prayer-as-weapon, Torah/souls, the covenant, or the zivug domain. This is consistent with the Torah's focus: it is primarily a positive teaching about how prayer works, with only a brief negative section on what corrupts it.
